The “and” here describes a condition: matter would then have no form capable of acting as a cause. It would lack the stable side through which existence can be given. As we have seen, form is the channel through which existence reaches matter, so this does not rule out a form that passes away. The form meant here is what makes a thing actual. If all coming-to-be were undone and things flowed back toward matter, that would be a return toward potentiality. Just as a soul can become like an active intellect by drawing close to it, a body can be said to return toward matter by approaching that limit.

The “veil” is the imagined division between one stage of change and another, which philosophers call the subject of motion. Mystics speak of these divisions as divine self-disclosures. They exist in thought, not as separate breaks in reality, because motion is one continuous process. The stages are so close together that the dividing line nearly disappears.

The Qur'anic verse about the people of Paradise receiving fruits that resemble one another comes from a passage about the forms of the afterlife. Ibn Arabi applies it here to the similar forms that appear successively during a person's ascent. Seen by God's light, these stages resemble heavenly forms. As a person's love and insight grow, manifestations of God's acts give way to manifestations of His attributes and then His essence.
“In length and breadth” refers to the world and the afterlife: the afterlife lies within the world, as its inner dimension.

The manuscript may properly include the conjunction “and.” Even without it, the point is clear: since coming into being depends on a being that brings things about, God continually turns toward creation.
The shorter version of this proof relies only on the difference between speed and slowness: speed covers a longer distance in a shorter time, and slowness the reverse.

This is Avicenna's natural-philosophy proof for time, given in The Physics of The Book of Healing. It shows that each individual motion has its own individual time, distinct from the time of other motions, just as each body has its own measure. Each time can serve as a unit by which other motions are measured. The common time measured by the daily motion is a human convention because it is regular and familiar. Mulla Sadra also holds that a natural time, involved in the existence of events, is the measure of the whole bodily nature's substantial motion.
This is one of the proofs for substantial motion.

The author points to his view that nature is renewed. Other philosophers say that time measures the changing position of the heavenly sphere; Sadra says that it measures the renewal of celestial nature, since other natures do not change with the same regularity. In this account, nature has quantity as an inseparable feature, just as existence is inseparable from what exists. Or the meaning may be that time is the connected, nonlasting quantity of nature itself—the account previously attributed to other philosophers.
The wording is unclear, because if time is a quantity, it cannot be a substance.

This is a division of the whole into its parts. The options about whether time measures a material substance or its renewal depend on whether we view time and motion as the same in existence or distinct in concept. Sadra later reconciles the different views of time. Their relation resembles that of mathematical body to natural body: the measured extension is the same, but it is considered in two different ways. If time and nature are one in existence, time is the measure of a substance. If they are distinct in concept and in how they appear to thought, time is the measure of nature's renewal and motion, or of what belongs to a body.
Because its changing states include renewed stages of before and after, it would need another motion and another time, and another agent to bring that about.

The five or six features listed for the body that time measures come from the old idea of an outermost sphere: a round body surrounding the physical universe whose daily motion marks common time. It has since become clear that the celestial bodies imagined in that account do not exist. These features can instead apply to the universal bodily nature, whose substantial motion marks a common, substantial time. The everyday time we use is a convention based on the Earth's daily rotation.

If the body that time measures were removed, its replacement would also have to come before or after it in time, since matter that is formed from it or changed into it would itself be earlier or later.

This means that it must come before other bodies in both time and place. Its priority in place would be lost if it moved, or if something else moved toward it, since changes in amount and quality also depend on motion in place. Its priority in time would be lost if another body or another motion came before it. It would also fail to endure if it could change in amount, expand, contract, heat up, or cool down; each of these changes requires matter that can come to be and pass away. This follows if the author's wording is read as it stands. If “its breaking apart” refers to time, the point is even clearer.

The note means conceptions of goals. A conception of an end can itself move an agent to act, as the idea of sitting moves someone to make a bed. The reference is not to conceptions of positions or motions, or to features that follow from motion as incidental results; the word “proper” excludes those.

This is the immediate goal; the more remote goal is likeness to the higher principles. One objection is that motion is itself an action, so it cannot be the goal of its own action; another is that motion is a seeking, not something sought. The commentator replies that Avicenna may mean the goal of the sphere's existence, nature, and circular tendency. Avicenna says “the goal in motion,” not “the goal of motion.”

The individual produced by a particular nature is only an incidental goal in this example. The example concerns particularity: the proper goal of a particular nature is its own completion, including the completion of its matter. Everything aims at itself and at its own perfection.

The conceptions agree or differ because of the positions they represent. Positions encountered during one revolution are different in kind; positions repeated in later revolutions resemble earlier ones in kind, but are not the same individual position. A person turning in place encounters many different positions before returning to the starting point; the repeated positions are like the earlier ones. The contrast also applies to different celestial configurations, such as triangular and six-sided arrangements, conjunctions and oppositions. Here “conceptions” means perceptions of positions, not ideas of goals.
The conceptions would have to resemble each other in every respect. Still, “resembling” is loose wording, since two things can resemble each other without being identical.

The phrase includes the elemental substances whose positions necessarily follow from them. Knowing a thing also means knowing what necessarily follows from it. These forms arrive gradually and continuously: they have one connected existence, yet many kinds or individuals, as colors appear in succession on fruit during a change of quality.

Mathematical extension, which can be divided in thought, is one of the features that follow from a natural body without being affected by it. Position—the arrangement of parts in relation to one another—is part of the body's existence and identity. A body's existence cannot be without position or arrangement. Change in position is therefore the very change in the body's substantial existence. “Inseparable” here means not later than the body in existence. Even if positions are later features, their renewal shows that the body's nature is renewed too, since a changing effect points to a changing immediate cause.
The sphere's different places are counted through its positions or times. In itself, the sphere has one natural place and no motion from place to place.

This develops substantial motion from principles accepted by Avicenna and his followers. Since the sphere's natural place and position do not change into something unnatural, its nature must itself be renewed: each degree of position and place corresponds to a degree of nature. In one view, both nature and its effect are one when considered as continuing; when considered as divided into stages, each has connected parts. Another possibility is that the sphere changes position by its own will. Since each position is wanted and then left, the sphere's motion may be voluntary, even if nature is what acts directly. Avicenna elsewhere calls it natural.

This proposal aims to connect the many renewed positions to one stable nature. It also avoids the objection that renewed accidents show their source is renewed, and avoids making the natural place and position multiple. The commentator compares it to the common sense: the shared sense receives many different images, but is one power.

The two objections share one basis. One uses the rule that a universal nature has no existence by itself: the individual exists, and the universal exists only through its individual instance. The other uses the primacy of existence over essence. The commentator notes that each school has its own starting point.

Sadra is identifying the cause of time. The words “as one individual” point out that time itself makes the sphere an individual, or is inseparable from its individuality. So how could the sphere cause time? Calling it an “unrestricted cause” leaves open the possibility that it is an incomplete cause, such as a receptive subject, but the author denies that it is time's agent. A cause cannot itself be qualified by its effect. Since every body is in time, and substantial motion makes a body flow and pass away in its existence, the sphere cannot be an eternal cause of time.
“Shape” is added after the more specific features as a general example.

One might object that motion occurs only in some accidents. The reply is that all the world's accidents are unstable, but in different ways: the four named categories are directly flowing in existence; time, acting, and being acted upon are flowing in their meaning; and relations are flowing only because they depend on other things.
That is, time is renewed through the celestial body's renewal.
The phrase refers back to the claim that the body itself is the source and cause of directions and places, as the same argument shows explicitly.
“Precede by nature” is used in the broad sense of priority, including causal priority, rather than only the narrow sense of an incomplete cause.

If separate intellects and souls are the surest paths to God, then a cause that acts through position cannot be the source of their existence. Their cause must be immaterial and ultimately be the Necessary Being. The note also points out that time and place are renewed effects, not causes that exist before one another.
If the earlier and later cannot coexist by their own nature, they are times. If they cannot coexist only because of an incidental feature, they are things that exist in time.
This note connects the phrase “only God” to the earlier proof that a cause cannot depend in its existence on what it causes.

A sequence of causes can be allowed if its parts follow one another continuously. But a sequence of separate instants or disconnected times cannot be allowed. The commentator also gives a simpler proof: if circular motion began with an eternal God, its beginning would require a prior condition, and that condition another, without end.

Assuming that causes are connected and successive has led to the very things we were assuming did not yet exist: time and motion. The connected reality that changes is bodily nature; its continuous extension is motion, and time measures that extension. The stable middle that runs from beginning to end is motion considered as continuing, and the flowing instant is the setting in which this continuity is present.
“Intellectual” here means a real substance that exists in actuality, not merely an essence in the mind. On this reading it could include God.

One might ask how the sphere's highest soul can be the cause of time if the argument excludes the soul. The reply is that the soul causes time through its intellectual, unified side; the side attached to the body is its changing nature. The excluded cause is an independent bodily cause.

Creation, considered as creation, is new because it is renewal and change; these are forms of incompleteness and do not come from God as a separate thing. What God brings about is the existence in which this renewal occurs. The Qur'an says that God's command is done, not that God's created world is done.
The question has already been discussed, but here Sadra reviews the argument, tests it, and states his own position more fully.
What belongs to a thing essentially is not explained by a further cause; what belongs to it accidentally needs a cause. The original argument treats renewal as essential to motion.
A separate act of “coming-to-be” cannot be added as another cause. Otherwise, it too would need to come to be, and the chain could not connect changing things to continuous motion.

The commentator allows that the earlier philosophers may have meant that motion's existence is renewed, rather than that renewal is part of its essence; this would answer Sadra's first objection. The second objection applies to both sides, and they answer it by appealing to the stable, middle motion that maintains circular motion as one whole. The remaining disagreement is whether this perpetual circular motion really exists.

The commentator strongly defends the earlier philosopher's argument. The philosopher may mean “a renewed position,” rather than “renewal of position.” Sadra's disagreement is about the renewal of the celestial nature itself. Apart from that point, the earlier argument can be defended; some of the disagreement is about wording.

This recalls the familiar point that coming-to-be is not a separate thing: it is the coming-to-be of a thing. Otherwise, that new “coming-to-be” would itself need a further beginning, leading to an endless chain. The same is true of motion. On Sadra's account, motion is the existence of the natural world.

Motion cannot come before an actual event in the order of nature while occurring at the same time as it. Each part of motion is itself passing away, so it cannot remain alongside its effect. Motion is potential, while the event that has come to be is actual. Only something free of potentiality can give actuality. The true source is separate and stronger than the bodily effect; motion is instead the condition that determines when the event occurs. The cause is eternal—God or the Active Intellect—and the later condition is a segment of the sphere's circular motion.

The lasting feature of movement cannot mean merely that new positions keep replacing one another. That succession has no separate existence over and above its parts, so it cannot by itself provide the enduring link to an eternal cause. The earlier critic therefore took the claim to require a stable basis within motion and objected that a purely changing process cannot have one.

But the lasting basis intended here is motion considered as a passage between its beginning and end. In this sense, the movement is one continuous reality, even while its changing positions come and go. This is what the author meant earlier by saying that the continuous and enduring aspect of movement is its passage between the two limits.

Many philosophers use this distinction to explain how things that begin can depend on an eternal cause. Circular motion, considered as one ongoing passage, is related to the lasting cause; considered through its endlessly changing positions and relationships, it is connected with changing events. What changes is thus linked through what changes, and what endures through what endures.
First, the earlier philosopher means that the remote agent—the First Cause or an eternal intellect—is beginningless. The nearby cause and subject of celestial motion are not.

Sadra may be answering that essential renewal needs no separate cause, since what is essential is not caused. But he is also distinguishing the renewal itself from the existence that is renewed: although renewal is not separately caused, the existence in which it occurs is brought about by a cause.

The point applies broadly, but time, motion, circles, and powers are especially useful examples. Their intellectual forms are very different from their sensory or imagined forms. A gradual, particular existence is unlike the general, unified reality the intellect grasps; prime matter is pure potentiality, while its intellectual concept is an abstract universal. Water, fire, and separate intellects are more readily understood in both general and particular forms.
This is the same problem raised earlier about how a changing thing can depend on an eternal source, now stated in a simpler form.
An unstated premise is that anything produced without a prepared receiver must be a separate, immaterial form. Prime matter does not count as such a receiver because it has no actual form of its own.
If the receiver itself came to be, there would be a break at the beginning of the supposedly continuous renewal of nature. The account would then need to explain what came before that break.

The regress is not merely a succession of causes, which some philosophers allow. The receiver in question is the actual bearer of a form, not the earlier bearer of its potentiality. It exists together with the form it receives, so the argument would produce an endless chain of causes existing together.

If the receiver is assumed to be eternal, the argument must still distinguish the case where it is sufficient to receive the form from the case where it is not. The question cannot be answered merely by assuming the receiver's eternity.

An eternal receiver that is sufficient for the form would make that form fixed, not renewed. If the receiver and giver are present throughout, every stage of the form would be present together. Also, the question assumes no succession of preparations in matter; without such succession, there can be no succession of levels in the form. The original argument divides the cases into four: no receiver, a new receiver, an eternal receiver with no changing readiness, and an eternal receiver with changing readiness.
The claim that matter is eternal is rejected by anyone trying to show that the whole world began. It would also imply an eternal matter for each kind, and possibly for each individual form.
The challenge can be repeated for each specific form of each kind, and then for each particular form, leading to as many eternal matters as there are forms.
Every specific readiness needs something that makes it ready. Matter has a general, distant potentiality; a particular form gives it the specific, immediate potentiality for one kind of change.

The upshot of this account is that bodily nature changes in its very being. It remains constant in being changeable, so it can depend on a cause that does not change. These bodily natures are not separate existences: in their flowing reality they are one continuous, substantial nature. To say that this flowing nature is given to matter means that its existence includes a side of lack and nonexistence. Matter is not something separate from it that is already fully actual; that would be a contradiction.

On this understanding, the distinctions between bodily forms—fire, water, and the others—are like the distinctions between the parts of a motion. We divide and name them in thought; they are not cut apart in existence. Their effects nevertheless differ, as earlier differs from later and stronger from weaker. Each stage of this flowing nature has its particular degree and place through what it is. Just as one part of a journey comes before another because of its own position in the journey, no extra cause is required to give each stage its order.

That is how bodily natures stand when considered in their continuously changing existence. When we instead consider the kinds that the mind distinguishes, fire differs from air and a human being from a horse, each with its own features and effects. Each particular form requires matter prepared to receive it. A previous form, together with other preparing conditions, gives matter the readiness for the next; the previous form ceases when the next appears. Each new event is thereby connected with its eternal cause through conditions that themselves arise. Those different conditions follow from successive parts of one uninterrupted motion. Together with the corresponding stretch of time and the eternal cause, a particular stage of that motion makes up a complete cause for the new effect.

Prime matter is not one numerically distinct receiver that must be either wholly new or wholly eternal. Its unity is generic, as a kind is shared through its forms. We can say it is new in the sense that its substantial existence is renewed with the forms united to it, not in the sense that it was once absent and then appeared as one event. Or we can call it eternal in the sense that this renewal never stops—not in the sense that it remains fixed or has no cause. Its unity is one identity with many levels, not one fixed state. This is especially clear if matter and form are understood as united in existence: pure potentiality has no fixed actuality that would prevent it from receiving any form.

All readiness, nonexistence, and deficiency belong to matter, which is one reality because pure potentiality has no distinctions within itself. This keeps deficiencies from being attributed to God. Every actuality, existence, and perfection comes from the source of actuality and good; evil does not come from it.

This suggests that we may choose the first answer if we consider specific forms as absorbed in their separate intellectual forms, or focus on the lasting root within them, like the middle motion within a complete path or the flowing instant within time. In this respect, the forms are creative acts, not dependent on earlier matter, readiness, time, or nonexistence. The natural world as a whole is brought from nothing into being; material and temporal things, by contrast, are considered together with their matter and time.
Because prime matter is pure potentiality and has no specific readiness of its own, any general form is enough to make it actual.

“For it” means the potentiality belonging to a form that is itself clothed in potentiality, such as a form's subject. “On it” means the potentiality belonging to the form that matter can receive. The final option is potentiality for a further perfection. These are alternatives, not mutually exclusive examples.
Although matter is what can receive forms, it is equally open to every form. A specific form is therefore needed to give it the particular readiness for one particular form.
As noted earlier, existences may differ in their basic reality, and sometimes the feature that distinguishes them is the same feature they share.

This comparison concerns kinds as essences and the additional features that distinguish individuals within a kind. Looked at as actual existences, individual things also differ by degrees of existence; Sadra has already used such differences to argue for substantial motion.

A connected whole is one individual reality because its continuity gives it one identity. It has no separate parts until the mind inserts a boundary. Any point we choose can divide it, and there is no final smallest division. A line of any length—even one imagined as endless—is one individual while its continuity remains unbroken.
This makes bodily nature four-dimensional: it has length, width, depth, and time.

An unbounded spatial extension considered without a particular limit is a natural body. When it is considered with a definite limit, it is mathematical extension, the body's measured size. Similarly, when bodily nature's renewal is considered without a particular time limit, it is motion; when measured by a year, month, or hour, it is time.

This reflects the view of Avicenna and Sadra. Some philosophers distinguish two kinds of continuity in a body: substantial continuity, which makes it a body able to receive three dimensions, and accidental continuity, which makes quantity divisible into parts sharing boundaries.

Time belongs to motion as a feature considered in thought, and motion belongs to nature in the same way. They are features of nature that are not later than it in existence. This resembles individuality as a feature of existence: existence, unity, and individuality are all present through one reality.

The argument against time is that the past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the indivisible present cannot itself be time. The everyday present is part of the past or future. If the time in the mind is fixed, it is not time; if it flows, it is only the present. The reply is that time exists as a flowing reality, like the continuous middle of motion, which cannot be divided into past and future. A connected path of motion and its measure, time, also exist because their source exists; “existence” includes both a thing and what is real through it.

This may refer to the theologians' “imagined time,” which they say exists only as a mental measure before the world, with God's eternal existence as its source. Or it may refer to time that is merely imagined and has no source in reality. Both views are false: eternal, changeless existence cannot be the source of an extension that does not remain fixed.

This view does not give a single, consistent measure of time. One event can be called the time of another—sunrise for someone's arrival, a person's arrival for someone's death—and the reverse could be said too. A familiar or prominent event may serve as a sign for a time, but the event itself is not time. It is the period in which two events occur together, and their being together is itself temporal.

This view treats time as the spiritual, eternal age, or as the shared reality of separate intellects, which are beyond matter. Their qualities are their very existence, though not their essences. Some who call time necessary in itself may be thinking of that higher, luminous aspect of existence.

Avicenna rejects the claim that time is the outermost sphere by pointing out that the argument's middle term shifts: bodies are “in” time, but the sphere is not “in” itself in the same sense. The commentator notes that the intended syllogism may be different, but it still has a weak form.

Avicenna rejects the claim that time is motion because some things contain a past and a future without being time, such as a flood or the Resurrection. The commentator adds that motion, like a natural body, is an extension; time, like mathematical body, is its measure. Only when motion is measured can it be divided into past and future. Their claim that we notice time only when we sense motion is weak: failing to notice motion also makes us fail to notice many other things, but that does not make time identical to them.
Avicenna argues that one revolution cannot be time, since each part of time is itself time, while part of a revolution is not another revolution.

The commentator objects to the claim that time is the measure of existence. Existence is too exalted and broad to be measured by body or motion, since it includes immaterial beings that precede place, time, and direction. If “existence” means one particular thing that exists, then its measure is simply motion. The note criticizes the view as an imprecise use of philosophical language.

Here “everlasting age” is used in the ordinary, broad sense of the whole temporal series being present to God at once. In that sense, the technical everlasting age is already included in the first relation described.
This means considering each changing thing as present together with each stage of another changing thing.

The commentator says Plato and Aristotle need not disagree: time is plainly the measure of celestial motion. Calling time an independent, lasting reality may mean that the reality behind time is the everlasting age, and behind that, eternity. Time is the measure of changing things; the everlasting age is the sphere of stable, separate realities; eternity is the “container,” so to speak, of God's existence and attributes. Each level must remain distinct.
If past and future belong to changing things only incidentally, there must be something that has priority and posteriority in its own right. That thing is time.

God is not described as earlier or later in time, though He may be called prior in the sense of eternity, causation, or sustaining existence. Causation is one way His presence with things is understood.

People used to curse time when misfortune came, thinking time had brought it about. The saying answers that God, not time, brings events about. It may also mean that one should honor time because it is God's effect and the record of His creative act. Or it may refer to the universal intellects, whose existence belongs to God's realm; ordinary time is then a subtle reflection of that higher reality.

By the “fixed” the sages mean the universal intellects, filled with God's light and existing through Him. The relation of God to His names and knowledge is eternity; the relation of fixed knowledge to its changing objects is the everlasting age; and the relation among those changing objects is time. The commentator notes that some accounts reverse which side of the relation is being described.

Each motion has its own time: its amount measured by its speed. The familiar day is simply the standard people use to compare other motions. Some motions begin or end, but the argument applies to the universal motion that encompasses the bodily world—the substantial motion of bodily nature. The close reading shows that no motion can be preceded by a stretch of its own time. Universal motion therefore has no prior time.

Do not mistake this for saying that the world exists eternally in the same way God does. God and what belongs to His own realm are eternal and deserve the names of perfection; the things that receive existence are temporal and pass away. God is always giving, while what receives His gift is renewed and then passes on to another. Each moment He is at work; there is no repetition in the act of giving.

The surprising claim is that this natural world has no first time or last time, even though each particular body and motion comes to be in time and is surrounded by nonexistence. The reason is that bodily nature itself renews through substantial motion; it does not need some separate thing outside itself to mark its temporal beginning.

This is especially directed at those who imagine the world to have been preceded by a stretch of empty time, with nonexistence placed alongside existence. Once that temporal order is accepted, the conclusion follows.

Both problems arise from finding an order in these cases: between nonexistence and existence, and between God and each event. In both, the earlier and later cannot exist together in the relevant respect, so the order is temporal. The comparison with places outside the world does not work: a place can be finite without another place beyond it, but a newly existing thing must be preceded by nonexistence.

This is a second way to state the objection that every time needs a prior time. It also risks making all times exist together as container and contained, and thereby making time's parts fixed. Sadra replies that the priority is either essential, in which case the ordered items are parts of time and need no further time, or incidental, in which case they are things in time. The regress is successive, not a simultaneous chain.

“By its own nature” refers to time's existence, which relates it to what comes before and after. The first reply is that time would be a relation only if this relation belonged to its concept; it belongs instead to its existence. The second reply distinguishes the concept of priority, which belongs to the category of relation, from the actual existence that makes something prior or later. That existence is not itself a relation.
